chapter.name: Fractions in Disguise
chapter.blurb: Percentages as fractions with denominator 100 and their equivalence with decimals and ratios; finding a percentage of a quantity and working backward to find the whole; percentages greater than 100%; comparing proportions with different totals and computing percentage increase or decrease; profit, loss, discount and tax (GST) on cost price, marked price and selling price; simple annual interest without compounding versus with compounding (p(1+rt) and p(1+r)^t) and depreciation as repeated percentage decrease; and combining successive percentage changes such as stacked discounts or a markup followed by a discount.

scope_in.item: Define percentage as 'per hundred', state that the % symbol traces to the Latin 'per centum', and recognise a percentage as a fraction whose denominator is fixed at 100 (x% = x/100)
Express a fraction as a percentage by finding an equivalent fraction with denominator 100, or by multiplying the fraction by 100 (e.g. solving 3/4 = x/100)
Express a given percentage as a fraction in simplest form (e.g. 24% = 24/100 = 6/25), and state that a percentage z% can be written as any fraction equivalent to z/100
Convert a decimal to a percentage and back by multiplying or dividing by 100 (shifting the decimal point two places)
Compare two fractions or proportions that have different denominators by converting both to percentages first, to judge which is larger
Convert a percentage to per-mille (per 1000) or per-decem (per 10) notation as an extension of the same 'fixed denominator' idea used for per cent (per 100)
Convert a given ratio (e.g. millet to water) into a percentage of the total, and use that percentage to find the actual quantity of one part in a given total volume or weight
Find y% of a given quantity by computing (y/100) x quantity, including via proportional reasoning (e.g. 25:100 :: s:120) as an alternative to direct multiplication
Use benchmark percentages for mental computation -- 25% as a quarter, 50% as a half, 10% by dividing by 10 -- and build up other percentages from these benchmarks (e.g. 20% = 2x10%, 25% = 20%+5%)
Given a percentage and the corresponding actual amount, find the total quantity (the whole) by solving the proportional equation, and use it to find a remaining/complementary amount
Recognise and compute percentages greater than 100%, expressing them also as an equivalent fraction or decimal greater than 1, such as sales exceeding a target

Compare two percentage-of-quantity expressions (e.g. '50% of 510' vs '50% of 515') using estimation or reasoning rather than full computation, and fill in missing values in a percent-part-whole bar model
Compare two proportions with different totals (e.g. marks out of different maximum marks) by first converting each to a percentage of its own total

Compute percentage increase or percentage decrease using (amount of change / original amount) x 100, and state that 'the new value is (100+x)% of the original' means the same as 'the value increased by x%'
Read percentage values off a bar/column graph comparing categories, and judge whether given comparison statements about the graph are true or false
Define cost price (CP), marked price (MP) and selling price (SP), and compute profit or loss in rupees as SP-CP (or CP-SP), then as a percentage of the cost price
Distinguish profit percentage calculated on the cost price from profit percentage calculated on the selling price for the same transaction, and compute both for a given CP and SP
Distinguish gross profit (revenue minus cost of goods) from net profit (gross profit minus other expenses), and compute the net profit percentage on revenue
Compute the selling price after a stated percentage discount on the marked price, or find the marked price/cost price given the discount percentage and selling price
Compute the final price after adding a stated tax percentage (e.g. GST) to a price, or verify whether a stated tax amount on a bill is correct
Interpret an annual interest rate stated as 'r% p.a.' on a principal, and compute the amount after 1 year as principal + (r% of principal)
Compute the total amount after t years at a given annual rate WITHOUT compounding (interest paid out each year, principal unchanged) using amount = p(1 + rt), with r as the rate written as a decimal

Compute the total amount after t years at a given annual rate WITH compounding (interest added back to the principal each year) using amount = p x (1 + r)^t, and compare it against the without-compounding amount for the same p, r and t
Apply repeated annual percentage growth (compounding) to word problems on population growth or bacterial growth over a small whole number of years/hours
Compute depreciation of a value by a given annual percentage as repeated multiplication by (1-r), for one year or over several periods, rounding intermediate values sensibly

Compare two ways of arriving at a similar-looking total discount (e.g. a flat rupee discount vs. a percentage discount, or two successive percentage discounts vs. one combined percentage discount) by computing both on the same starting price

Apply a percentage markup to a cost price to get a selling price, then apply a percentage discount to that marked-up selling price, and find the resulting net profit or loss percentage on the original cost price

Solve mixed multi-step word problems that combine two or more percentage ideas from the chapter, such as a discount followed by a tax, or successive yearly percentage changes such as two different annual fare increases
Compare 'x% of y' with 'y% of x' for the same two numbers and recognise, including by a short algebraic argument, that the two are always equal
Convert a 'buy m, get n free' offer into an effective percentage discount by comparing the number of items paid for against the number of items received

scope_out.reason: A stand-alone chess/knight-placement puzzle on p. 32 with no percentage content of its own to be tested

scope_out.item: Quarterly, half-yearly or monthly compounding of interest
scope_out.reason: Every compounding example in this chapter compounds annually (p.a.); no sub-annual compounding period is introduced or computed

scope_out.item: The formal terms 'Simple Interest' and 'Compound Interest', or the R/100-style textbook formulas SI = PRT/100 and CI = P(1+R/100)^n - P
scope_out.reason: These exact terms never appear in this chapter. The book deliberately says 'without compounding' and 'with compounding' instead, and writes the rate r as a decimal proportion (e.g. 0.10) rather than as R% divided by 100 inside the formula

scope_out.item: GST slabs, CGST/SGST splitting, or any tax structure beyond adding one flat percentage to a price
scope_out.reason: The chapter shows GST only as a single percentage added on top of a price (e.g. 18% on a phone) and asks students to verify a bill; no slab rates or tax-type breakdown is taught

scope_out.item: Formal business costing such as fixed vs. variable costs, or overheads as a named category
scope_out.reason: Gross and net profit are illustrated with one example each of 'other expenses' lumped together; no costing framework beyond that single worked example is taught

scope_out.item: The specific real-world percentage facts in the 'Percentages Around Us' trivia box (body water content, ice cream air content, World Cup viewership, etc.)
scope_out.reason: These are general-knowledge illustrations of where percentages appear in real life, not numbers the chapter teaches students to derive or compute with

scope_out.item: Finding the number of years or terms needed for an investment to reach a target amount (solving for t or n)
scope_out.reason: Every worked example and exercise gives t directly and asks for the amount; none asks the student to solve p(1+r)^t = target for t

scope_out.item: Ratio and proportion as a topic in its own right (simplifying ratios, the Rule of Three, dividing a quantity in a given ratio)
scope_out.reason: Covered in full in Part I chapter 7 (Proportional Reasoning-1); this chapter only uses a ratio incidentally, to convert it to a percentage (e.g. the millet:water mixture on p. 9), never to solve a proportion problem for its own sake

concepts.name: Fractions, Decimals, Ratios and Percentages
concepts.description: Converting between fractions, decimals, ratios and percentages in both directions, and understanding why percentages use a fixed denominator of 100.
concepts.idea: A percentage is just a fraction whose denominator is fixed at 100, so converting between fraction, decimal, ratio and percentage is the same idea seen four ways.
concepts.rule: To write a fraction or ratio as a percentage, multiply it by 100. To write x% as a fraction, write it as x/100 and simplify. A decimal is converted to a percentage by multiplying by 100 (shifting the decimal point two places right), and back by dividing by 100.
concepts.example: 3/4 of the paint mixture is red, so as a percentage this is 3/4 x 100 = 75%; equivalently 0.75 = 75%.

concepts.name: Percentage of a Quantity, and Percentages Greater Than 100
concepts.description: Finding y% of a quantity, working backward to find the whole given a part and its percentage, and understanding percentages greater than 100%.
concepts.idea: Finding y% of a quantity means multiplying the quantity by y/100; the same relationship can run backward to find the whole when only a part and its percentage are known, and percentages are not capped at 100 when the part exceeds the whole.
concepts.rule: y% of a quantity Q is (y/100) x Q. If a% of an unknown whole equals a known value k, the whole is k divided by (a/100). A percentage greater than 100% means the part is larger than the whole it is being compared to.
concepts.example: 40% of a 230 km trip is 92 km; equivalently, if 92 km is known to be 40% of the trip, the whole trip is 92 / 0.4 = 230 km. Selling goods worth 6000 against a target of 5000 is 120% of the target.

concepts.name: Comparing Proportions and Percentage Increase/Decrease
concepts.description: Comparing quantities that have different totals by converting each to a percentage, and computing percentage increase or decrease.
concepts.idea: Percentages let two quantities with different totals be compared fairly by putting both on a common scale of 100, and the same idea measures how much a quantity has grown or shrunk relative to where it started.
concepts.rule: To compare two scores or proportions out of different totals, convert each to a percentage of its own total first. Percentage increase or decrease = (amount of change / original amount) x 100; 'increased by x%' and 'is (100 + x)% of the original' describe the same relationship.
concepts.example: 42 out of 50 is 84%, while 70 out of 80 is 87.5%, so the second is proportionally higher. Tomatoes rising from 30 to 42 rupees per kg is a (12/30) x 100 = 40% increase.

concepts.name: Profit, Loss, Discount and Tax
concepts.description: Cost price, marked price and selling price; profit and loss percentage on cost price and on selling price; gross vs net profit; discount; and tax such as GST added to a price.
concepts.idea: Profit, loss, discount and tax are all differences between two rupee amounts, and expressing that difference as a percentage of the right base (cost price, marked price, or revenue) makes deals comparable regardless of the amounts involved.
concepts.rule: Profit % (on cost) = (SP - CP)/CP x 100; Loss % (on cost) = (CP - SP)/CP x 100; a discount is subtracted from the marked price to give the selling price; a tax such as GST is added on top of a price as a percentage of that price.
concepts.example: Buying at 300 and selling at 430 rupees is a profit of 130, which is (130/300) x 100 = 43.3% on the cost price; a 35% discount on an 1800-rupee MRP brings the selling price down to 0.65 x 1800 = 1170 rupees.

concepts.name: Interest, Compounding and Depreciation
concepts.description: Simple annual interest without compounding, interest with compounding, the formulas p(1+rt) and p(1+r)^t, and depreciation as repeated percentage decrease.
concepts.idea: Money invested at a fixed annual rate grows by the same rupee amount every year if the interest is paid out each time (without compounding), but grows by an increasing rupee amount if the interest is left in and added to the principal (with compounding); a value that depreciates loses a fixed percentage of whatever it is currently worth, which is compounding in reverse.
concepts.rule: Without compounding, the amount after t years is p(1 + rt); with compounding, it is p(1 + r)^t, where p is the principal and r is the annual rate written as a decimal. Depreciation or a repeated decrease by r each period multiplies the current value by (1 - r) every period.
concepts.example: 6000 rupees at 10% p.a. for 3 years without compounding gives 6000 x 1.3 = 7800 rupees; with compounding it gives 6000 x 1.1^3 = 7986 rupees. A 21,000-rupee TV depreciating 5% in a year is worth 0.95 x 21,000 = 19,950 rupees.

concepts.name: Successive Percentage Changes
concepts.description: Combining two or more percentage changes applied one after another to the same quantity, such as successive discounts or a markup followed by a discount.
concepts.idea: Two or more percentage changes applied one after another to the same quantity do not simply add up, because each later change acts on the new, already-changed value rather than on the original.
concepts.rule: To combine successive percentage changes, apply each one in turn as a multiplying factor on the running value (a 30% discount then a 20% discount is x0.7 then x0.8, not a single 50% discount); a markup followed by an equal-looking discount does not return to the original price.
concepts.example: A 200-rupee cake given a 30% discount then a further 20% discount costs 200 x 0.7 x 0.8 = 112 rupees, more expensive than a single 50% discount, which would bring it to 100 rupees.
